descs.en: She married the arms dealer to protect her father. He has never stopped wondering whether she married him for love.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lin Elowen is a florist in the Walled City. Her father moves cargo for Zhao Zhendong, the arms dealer the whole city is afraid of. When three of Zhao’s containers are seized and her father is blamed, Elowen walks into Zhao’s office at the Iron Docks and does something nobody expects.

She asks him to marry her.

It is a contract, three pages long, in her neat handwriting. Separate rooms. Her own shop. You don’t touch me unless I ask. He signs it without arguing. He knows exactly why she wants him, and it isn’t love.

Every Flower in the Shop is a slow-burn romance inside a marriage: a woman who married a dangerous man to protect her family, and a man who would burn the world down for her and still can’t bring himself to ask the one question that matters. Did she ever choose him at all?

Main chapters tell the story in order, in four volumes. Side stories will come between volumes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a dark romance. The love story is tender, but the world around it is not. Volume One includes:

• The illegal arms trade, discussed throughout

• Violence heard off the page: a man’s fingers broken (The Florist Who Read His Shipping Routes)

• A man badly beaten in revenge, mentioned (A Proposal Made Like a Business Deal)

• Unwanted touching at a dinner table, and a stabbing through the hand (The First Dinner as Mrs. Zhao)

• Arson, serious burns, and a man burned on purpose as revenge (The Night the Delivery Van Burned)

• Grief for a parent who died in childbirth

• A love scene between the married couple. It is sensual but not explicit (Page Two, Line Six)

Later volumes will include gun violence, killing, and a long, frightening disappearance. Warnings will be added as they are published.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
After The Softest Kind of Love, I wanted to write the other kind: a love that is quiet because it is so big, between two people who are not soft at all.

Zhao Zhendong is not a good man, and this book won’t pretend he is. Elowen knows exactly what he does. What she doesn’t know, for a long time, is what to do with the fact that the most frightening man in the city sits outside her bedroom door every night so she won’t have to wonder where he is.

The flower shop details are real: the 4 a.m. market, cutting stems with a knife at an angle, the cooler kept just above freezing. The arms trade is kept at the level of a story. Thank you for reading.

chapters.title: The Arms Dealer Who Bought Every Flower in the Shop
chapters.desc: A rainy closing time, a man waiting for her father, and a florist who did not flinch.
chapters.epigraph: “He came in out of the rain like he owned it. Then he asked how long the tulips would last.”
chapters.content:
The rain started at six, which meant nobody would come in after seven.

Lin Elowen knew the rhythm of the shop the way other people knew their own heartbeat. Morning was for brides and funerals. Lunch was for office workers who had forgotten a birthday. Late afternoon was for men who had done something wrong. And when it rained in the Walled City, the narrow streets filled with water and umbrellas and bad tempers, and the last hour before closing belonged to her.

She was twenty-four. The shop was five years old. The sign above the door said Elowen’s in white paint, because she had been nineteen and exhausted when she painted it and could not think of anything cleverer.

She was stripping the lower leaves from a bucket of white stock when the bell over the door rang.

“We close in ten minutes,” she said, without looking up. “If it’s for an apology, I recommend the peonies. They look expensive.”

Nobody answered.

She looked up.

The man in the doorway was soaked to the skin. His black coat was dark with rain, his hair flattened against his forehead, and water ran off him onto her clean floor in a steady, careless stream. He was tall and very still. Not the stillness of someone waiting politely. The stillness of a dog that has not decided whether to bite.

Behind him, through the glass, two more men stood under the awning of the noodle shop across the street. They were not eating noodles.

Elowen put down the stock.

She knew who he was. Everyone in her father’s house knew who he was, even if nobody said the name out loud. She had seen him once, three years ago, from the top of the stairs: a younger man in a cheap suit, standing in her father’s office, saying nothing while her father talked too fast.

Zhao Zhendong. The man who moved weapons the way her father moved rice and televisions. The man her father worked for.

“Miss Lin,” he said. His voice was lower than she remembered, a little rough, as if he did not use it often. “I’m looking for your father.”

“He isn’t here.”

“I know. His phone is off. His office is locked. His driver says he went home. He did not go home.” Zhao looked around the shop, slowly. Buckets of roses. Lilies in the cooler. Ribbon on the wall. A small radio playing old songs. “So I’ll wait here. He calls you every night at eight.”

Elowen felt something cold settle in her stomach.

It was true. Her father called every night at eight, wherever he was, to ask if she had eaten. She had never told anyone. Which meant someone had listened.

“You can’t wait here,” she said. “I’m closing.”

“Then stay open.”

“I have customers in the morning.”

“You don’t have any now.” He glanced at the window, at the rain, at the empty street. Then he reached into his coat, and every muscle in her body went tight.

He took out a wallet.

“How much,” he said, “for everything?”

She stared at him.

“Everything,” he repeated. “All the flowers. If I buy them, the shop is mine until eight. Nobody comes in. Nobody asks why there’s a man standing in a flower shop. You can go home, if you want. I won’t touch anything.”

It was such a strange thing to say that, for a moment, she forgot to be afraid.

She looked at the buckets. She did the sum without meaning to. She always did sums.

“Four thousand two hundred,” she said. “Wholesale cost, about fifteen hundred. The rest is my labour and the rent.”

He counted out five thousand in cash and put it on the counter, next to her scissors.

“I’m not going home,” Elowen said.

“Fine.”

“And you’re dripping on my floor.”

He looked down at the puddle spreading around his shoes. For the first time, something moved in his face, too quickly for her to read. Then he took off his wet coat, folded it over his arm, and stood on the doormat like a schoolboy who had been told off.

He was wearing a grey shirt under it. There was a holster under his left arm. He did not try to hide it.

Elowen picked up a towel from the workbench and threw it at him.

He caught it without looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first twenty minutes, neither of them said anything.

She finished the stock. She re-cut the roses that had come in that morning from the south, a sharp diagonal cut an inch from the bottom of each stem, dry, with a knife instead of scissors, because scissors crushed the stem and the flower would drink less. She dropped each one into a bucket of cold water with flower food. She checked the cooler. One degree. Good.

He watched her the whole time.

Not her body. Her hands.

“Why the knife?” he said at last.

She didn’t look up. “Scissors squash the stem. It can’t drink. It dies faster.”

“And the angle?”

“More surface to drink from. And it doesn’t sit flat on the bottom of the bucket.”

He was quiet for a moment. “Like a wound,” he said. “A clean cut heals. A crushed one doesn’t.”

Elowen’s knife paused.

She looked at him then. He was leaning against the wall beside the door, the towel around his neck, his coat still folded over his arm. He was younger than she had thought. Twenty-five, maybe. His knuckles were scarred. There was a thin white line through his left eyebrow.

“Yes,” she said slowly. “Like a wound.”

At seven forty, a woman knocked on the glass with an umbrella and pointed at the tulips.

Elowen glanced at Zhao.

He didn’t move. Didn’t speak. He only looked at the woman through the glass, and after a second, the woman lowered her umbrella and walked away very quickly.

“You scared her,” Elowen said.

“I bought the tulips.”

“She wanted them for her mother. It’s her mother’s birthday. She comes every year.”

He looked at her. Then he took the tulips out of their bucket, all twenty stems, dripping, walked to the door, and opened it into the rain.

“Hey,” he called. Not loudly. The woman stopped.

He held out the tulips.

The woman looked at the flowers, at his face, at the holster under his arm. She took the tulips with both hands, said something Elowen couldn’t hear, and ran.

Zhao came back in, shut the door, and stood on the doormat again. His sleeves were wet to the elbow.

“Those were my tulips,” Elowen said.

“They were my tulips. I paid.”

She opened her mouth to argue. Then she closed it, because he was right, and because she had just watched the most frightening man her father knew give away flowers to a stranger in the rain, and she didn’t know what to do with that.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight o’clock, her phone rang.

Zhao straightened.

Elowen looked at the screen. Baba. She let it ring twice. She looked at Zhao.

“If you hurt him,” she said, quietly, “I will find out where you sleep.”

It was a ridiculous thing to say. She was a florist. She was holding a rose.

He didn’t laugh.

“I don’t want to hurt him,” he said. “I want to know where my containers are.”

She answered the phone.

“Elowen,” her father said. He sounded tired. He always sounded tired lately. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet, Baba.” She kept her eyes on Zhao. “Mr. Zhao is here. In the shop.”

The silence on the other end lasted so long she thought the line had dropped.

Then, very softly, her father said, “Put him on.”

She held out the phone. Zhao crossed the shop in three steps and took it, and for the first time she saw his hands up close. Big, scarred, careful.

“Lin Jian,” he said.

She could hear her father’s voice, small and fast, through the speaker. She couldn’t make out the words. Zhao listened. He didn’t interrupt. Once he said, “When?” and once he said, “Who told you that?” and once, very flatly, “No.”

Then he said, “Two weeks. Then I come to your house. Not your office. Your house.”

He hung up and gave the phone back to her.

“Is he safe?” Elowen asked.

Zhao picked up his wet coat. He put it on. He looked around the shop again, at the buckets, at the roses, at the gap where the tulips had been.

“For two weeks,” he said.

He went to the door. Then he stopped, with his hand on the frame, and turned back.

“The flowers,” he said. “What happens to them?”

“They’re yours.”

“I can’t keep flowers. I don’t have anywhere to put them.” He said it like a fact, like I don’t have a car. “Sell them again tomorrow. Keep the money.”

“Then you’ll have paid for them twice.”

“Then it was a good night for you.” He pulled up his collar. “The delphiniums. The blue ones. Don’t put them near the door. The draught will make them drop.”

She stared at him.

“How do you know that?”

He almost smiled. It wasn’t quite a smile. It was the place where one would have been, if he’d had more practice.

“You told me,” he said. “About an hour ago. You were talking to yourself.”

Then he went out into the rain, and the two men under the noodle shop awning fell into step behind him, and the street swallowed them.

Elowen stood in the middle of her shop and didn’t move.

On the counter, next to her scissors, was five thousand in cash.

On the doormat, where he’d stood, was a perfect wet outline of two shoes.

She moved the delphiniums away from the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the back of the car, halfway to the Iron Docks, Zhao Zhendong looked down and saw a single blue floret stuck to the wet wool of his sleeve.

A delphinium. One small flower, no bigger than a fingernail, the colour of the sky right before it gets dark.

He should have brushed it off. Instead he peeled it away from the wool with two fingers, slowly, so it wouldn’t tear, and sat holding it on his palm while the city went past in streaks of rain.

In the front seat, Bao glanced in the mirror and very wisely said nothing.

Zhao opened his wallet and put the flower behind his identity card, flat, where it would stay dry.

It was still there on the morning he married her.

chapters.title: Lin Jian Owes Three Containers
chapters.desc: A seizure at the Iron Docks, two weeks to pay, and her father’s shaking hands.
chapters.content:
Her father came home at midnight, smelling of cigarettes he had promised to stop smoking.

Elowen was waiting in the kitchen. She had made congee because it was the only thing he would eat when he was worried, and she had been keeping it warm for two hours. The Lin house in the Walled City was old and tall and full of stairs, and at night every sound carried. She heard the gate. She heard the driver’s car pull away. She heard her father stop in the hall for a long time before he came in.

Lin Jian was fifty-three. Five years ago, he had looked forty. Tonight he looked older than her grandfather had at the end.

“You should be asleep,” he said.

“You should have called me back.”

He sat down at the kitchen table. She put the bowl in front of him. He didn’t pick up the spoon. His hands were on the table, and they were shaking, a small fast tremor he tried to hide by pressing his palms flat.

“What did he say to you?” Lin Jian asked.

“He bought every flower in the shop and gave the tulips to a stranger.” She sat down opposite him. “Baba. What did you lose?”

He laughed, a short, terrible sound.

“Three containers,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came out slowly, the way the truth always did in their house.

Lin Jian was not a criminal, he would have said. He was a logistics man. He arranged things. A shipping container needed a port, a ship, a customs broker, a warehouse, a truck, a driver who didn’t ask questions, and papers that said what everyone needed them to say. Lin Jian knew which forms went to which offices and which officers liked which brand of whisky at New Year. For twenty years he had moved anything anyone paid him to move: electronics, rice, medicine, cars with their engines taken out. For the last six years, the person paying him most had been Zhao Zhendong.

“What was in them?” Elowen asked.

Her father looked at the congee.

“Agricultural machinery,” he said.

She waited.

“That’s what the papers said.”

“And what was in them?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. She had grown up in this house. She had learned very young not to open the long boxes that sometimes sat in the garage overnight, and not to ask why some of her father’s visitors had accents from countries she couldn’t find on the map.

“They were seized at the Iron Docks,” Lin Jian said. “Customs opened all three. Not a random check. They went straight to them. They knew.”

“Someone told them.”

“Someone told them.” He rubbed his face. “Zhao’s buyer had already paid. Half up front. Now the buyer wants the money back or the goods delivered, and Zhao has neither, and in Zhao’s world, if you lose a man’s shipment, you are the one who pays for it.”

“How much?”

He told her.

Elowen had done sums her whole life. She had kept the household accounts since she was twelve, since the night her mother went into hospital to have Eliana and didn’t come home. She knew to the yuan what the house cost, what the shop made, what her brothers and sisters spent. The number her father said was not a number she could do anything with. It was the price of their house, and the shop, and everything in both of them, three times over.

“He gave you two weeks,” she said.

“He gave me two weeks to find out who sold the route. If I can’t find them, he’ll assume it was me.”

“It wasn’t you.”

“No.” Her father finally picked up the spoon. He held it without eating. “But a man like Zhao Zhendong doesn’t care what’s true, Elowen. He cares what’s useful.”

She thought about the man standing on her doormat with a towel around his neck. The way he had said like a wound. The way he had turned the woman with the umbrella back into the rain with a bunch of tulips.

“I don’t think that’s true,” she said.

Her father looked up sharply.

“Don’t,” he said. “Don’t you ever think about him like that. You see a man buying flowers. I see a man who once made a customs officer eat the paper he’d signed.” His voice cracked. “Promise me you’ll stay away from him.”

She didn’t promise. She took his bowl, warmed the congee again, and sat with him while he ate half of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning the whole house knew something was wrong, because nobody in the Lin family was good at pretending except Elowen.

Raiden came down to breakfast at seven, which was unheard of. He was twenty-two and played the cheerful, slightly useless son so well that most of their father’s associates thought he was simple. He wasn’t. He had walked back to this house alone at fourteen, across a border, from a safe house their father had hidden him in. He had memorised every room in the Walled City by sixteen.

“Baba didn’t go to the office,” Raiden said, stealing a dumpling from her plate. “He’s in the study with the door locked. He’s never in the study with the door locked.”

“He’s tired.”

“Jie.” He looked at her. He only called her jie, big sister, when he was serious. “The two men across the street from your shop last night. I saw them on the traffic camera. They were Zhao’s.”

Elowen kept eating. “You shouldn’t be looking at traffic cameras.”

“You shouldn’t be closing up alone with the Iron Docks in your shop.”

Evangeline came in then, quiet as always, and sat at the end of the table without a word. She was twenty-two too, on paper Raiden’s twin, which was a lie the whole family told so automatically they sometimes forgot it was one. She looked at Elowen’s face and then at Raiden’s and poured herself tea and said nothing, which in Evangeline’s language meant I know, and I’m scared too.

Elara was at university. Eliana, seventeen, was still asleep, or more likely awake upstairs with three computer screens open, listening to every word through a device she had built herself and thought nobody knew about.

Five children. One father with shaking hands. Two weeks.

Elowen finished her breakfast. She washed her plate. Then she went upstairs, past the study with its locked door, into the small room at the end of the corridor where her father kept the files he didn’t keep at the office.

She had known where the key was since she was fifteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The papers for the three containers were in a grey folder at the back of the bottom drawer.

She sat on the floor with them, her back against the filing cabinet, and read everything.

She didn’t understand all of it. Some of it was in shipping language: bills of lading, packing lists, a port schedule, a broker’s invoice. Some of it was in her father’s handwriting, small and slanted, the code he used for things he didn’t write down plainly. But she understood numbers, and dates, and the order things happened in.

Three containers. Loaded at a warehouse in the Iron Docks on the third. Booked onto a ship by a broker called Hengli Freight on the fourth. Seized on the ninth.

She took out a pencil and started making a list.

Who knew the container numbers? Her father. The warehouse manager. The broker. Zhao’s people.

Who knew the date of the inspection that never should have happened? Nobody. That was the point. Customs at the Iron Docks didn’t open containers without a reason. Somebody had given them one.

She went back further. There were older folders in the drawer, older shipments. She pulled out every one from the last two years, spread them across the floor, and started comparing them.

It took her four hours.

By the end, her legs were numb and the floor was covered in paper, and she had found it.

There had been two other seizures in the past eighteen months. Small ones. One container each. Her father had marked them both with a single red line and a word: bad luck.

They weren’t bad luck.

All three seizures had something in common, and it wasn’t her father. It wasn’t the warehouse or the broker or the ship. In each case, two days before the containers were seized, there was a note in her father’s handwriting about a phone call. The same initials, every time. Someone from Zhao’s side, ringing to “confirm details.”

K.

Elowen sat back against the filing cabinet and stared at the letter.

Then she gathered up every page, put them back exactly where they had been, and locked the drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell her father.

That was the first decision she made, sitting on the floor of that small room, and later she would think it was the moment everything else began. If she told him, he would go to Zhao himself. He would stand in that office at the Iron Docks with his shaking hands and try to explain that the leak was one of Zhao’s own men, and Zhao would look at him, a frightened fixer who had just lost three containers, accusing someone Zhao trusted.

A man like Zhao Zhendong doesn’t care what’s true. He cares what’s useful.

Maybe. But she had watched him ask why she used a knife instead of scissors, and listen to the answer.

That night, Elowen went to the shop at the usual time. She bought flowers at the market at four in the morning like always. She made two wedding bouquets and a funeral wreath and an apology arrangement for a man who had forgotten his anniversary. She smiled at customers.

At closing, she sat at her workbench with a cup of cold tea and the copy she had made, in her own handwriting, of three dates and one initial.

On the corner of the counter, under the till, were the five thousand in cash he had left. She hadn’t been able to make herself put it in the bank.

She picked up a pen and wrote a note to herself on the back of a delivery slip.

Iron Docks. Tomorrow. 10 a.m.

Then she sat looking at it until the tea was completely cold, because she knew that the moment she walked into that building, her life would split cleanly in two, like a stem under a sharp knife.

A clean cut heals, he had said.

She hoped he was right.

When she locked up that night, there was a black car parked across the street with its lights off.

It had been there every night since the rain. She had thought it was watching her. Standing on the wet pavement with her keys in her hand, she realised for the first time that it might be watching over her instead.

She didn’t know which frightened her more.

chapters.title: The Florist Who Read His Shipping Routes
chapters.desc: She walks into his office at the Iron Docks and tells him where his route broke.
chapters.content:
The Iron Docks did not smell like the sea. They smelled like rust and diesel and wet concrete, and underneath all of it something sour, like a coin held too long in a sweaty hand.

Elowen took two buses to get there. She wore her plainest coat and flat shoes, and she carried her handbag in front of her with both arms, like the women she’d seen at the market who had been robbed once and never forgot it. The cranes were enormous. Container stacks rose on both sides of the road in blocks of red and blue and grey, six high, like a city made by someone who had never seen a window.

Zhao Zhendong’s office was above a warehouse with a sign that said NORTHGATE INDUSTRIAL PUMPS in faded green letters. There were pumps in the window. They had dust on them.

The man at the door was the same one who had stood under the noodle shop awning two nights ago. He looked at her. He looked at her handbag.

“I need to see Mr. Zhao,” Elowen said. “Tell him it’s Lin Jian’s daughter. Tell him it’s about the containers.”

He didn’t move.

“Tell him,” she said, “that I know who sold the route.”

The man’s eyes changed. He took out a phone, turned away, and spoke three words into it. Then he held the door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

The office was not what she had expected.

She had imagined something like a film: dark wood, a big desk, a window over the harbour, maybe a tiger skin. Instead it was a long, bare room with a concrete floor and metal shelves full of binders. There was a desk, but it was covered in papers and a laptop and a half-eaten box of rice. A whiteboard on one wall was covered in numbers and arrows. Through a window at the back, she could see straight down into the warehouse, where men were moving pallets with a forklift.

Zhao was standing at the whiteboard with a marker in his hand. He was in shirtsleeves, the sleeves pushed to the elbow. The holster was there again. So was another man, sitting on the edge of the desk, eating sunflower seeds out of a paper twist.

He was in his forties, with a soft face and a good watch and the kind of smile that waiters trusted. He looked at Elowen with friendly interest.

“Lin Jian sent his daughter,” he said. “That’s new.”

“Kang,” said Zhao, without turning around. “Quiet.”

K.

Elowen’s heart did something painful in her chest. She kept her face still. She had a lot of practice keeping her face still.

Zhao capped the marker and turned. He looked tired, as if he hadn’t slept since the rain.

“You said you know who sold the route,” he said.

“I’d like to speak to you alone.”

Kang laughed. “Anything you can say to him, you can say to me, little sister. I’ve been with Zhao since he was carrying boxes.”

Zhao looked at Elowen, then at Kang.

“Kang stays,” he said.

So she did it the other way. She didn’t look at Kang. She took the folded paper out of her handbag, walked to the desk, moved the box of rice aside, and laid the paper flat in front of Zhao.

“There were three seizures,” she said. “Not one. The big one this month, and two small ones last year. My father wrote ‘bad luck’ next to the small ones. It wasn’t luck.”

She pointed with one finger, the way she pointed at an order sheet for a nervous bride.

“Each time, two days before customs opened the container, somebody from your side called my father to confirm the container number and the sailing date. Same person each time. My father wrote down the initial.” She didn’t say it. She didn’t look at the man on the edge of the desk. “Nobody else had all three things together. Not the warehouse, not the broker, not the ship. Only my father, and the person who called him.”

The room was quiet. Down in the warehouse, the forklift beeped as it reversed.

Zhao read the paper. He read it again. His face didn’t change at all.

Kang had stopped eating sunflower seeds.

“That’s Lin Jian’s handwriting copied by Lin Jian’s daughter,” he said. He was still smiling, but the smile had gone thin. “He lost your containers, Zhendong, and now his girl walks in here with a story about initials. Very convenient.”

“It is convenient,” Zhao agreed.

Elowen’s stomach turned over.

Zhao picked up his phone. He scrolled, pressed a name, and held it to his ear.

“Si,” he said. “I need phone records. One man. Both his numbers. The third, the seventeenth of last March, the twenty-ninth of last October.” A pause. “Yes. Now.”

He hung up.

“Sit down,” he said to Elowen. “It takes about an hour.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the longest hour of her life.

She sat on a metal chair by the shelves. Zhao went back to his whiteboard and wrote numbers she didn’t understand. Kang stayed on the edge of the desk. After ten minutes he started talking again, easily, about the weather and the price of diesel and a restaurant he liked in the old town, as if nothing was wrong. Nobody answered him. After twenty minutes, he stopped.

At thirty minutes, he stood up and said he was going to get cigarettes.

“Sit down,” said Zhao.

Kang sat down.

At fifty-two minutes, Zhao’s phone buzzed. He read the message. He read it twice.

Then he put the phone face down on the whiteboard ledge, and said, without turning around, “Miss Lin. Go downstairs and wait in the car by the door. Bao will drive you home.”

Elowen stood.

She would remember later that she had wanted to leave, very badly, and that her legs had not moved. She was looking at Kang, and Kang was looking at Zhao’s back, and his soft, friendly face had gone grey.

“Zhendong,” Kang said. “Brother. Listen. It wasn’t—they were going to take it anyway. The Qiu brothers. They already knew half of it, I only—”

“Bao,” said Zhao.

The man from the door was already beside her, his hand on her elbow. Not rough. Firm. He turned her toward the stairs.

She was on the third step down when she heard it.

She didn’t see it. She heard Kang start to say please, and she heard a sound like someone snapping a thick branch over their knee, and then a scream so high and so raw that it didn’t sound human. Then another sound, the same. Then the scream stopped being words.

Bao kept walking. His hand stayed steady on her elbow. At the bottom of the stairs, he opened the door to the yard and walked her out into the grey daylight, and only then did she realise she had been holding her breath the whole way down.

“Breathe,” Bao said, not unkindly. “In through the nose.”

She breathed.

Through the window above, she could see nothing. The forklift had stopped. The men in the warehouse had all turned their backs to the stairs, very deliberately, the way people turn away from a car accident when they know there’s nothing they can do.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out twenty minutes later.

She was sitting in the back of a black car with the door open, because she couldn’t stand to have it shut. Zhao walked across the yard toward her with his hands in his pockets. He had washed them. She could see the water still drying on his wrists. There was a small dark spot on the cuff of his shirt that hadn’t come out.

He stopped beside the open door and didn’t get in.

“Your father owes me nothing,” he said. “Tell him the debt is closed.”

She nodded. She didn’t trust her voice.

“Kang has been selling my routes to the Qiu brothers for two years,” he went on, flatly, as if reading a weather report. “They used them to embarrass me and take my buyers. They got your father’s name and his whole network with them. Every officer he pays, every warehouse, every driver.”

“What happens to Kang?”

He looked at her.

“He’s alive,” he said. “He won’t hold a pen again.”

Elowen looked down at her own hands in her lap. They were steady. She didn’t understand how.

“You should have sent me out sooner,” she said.

“Yes.” He didn’t apologise. He didn’t explain. After a moment, he said, quieter, “I didn’t think you would stay.”

“I didn’t either.”

He crouched down beside the car, so that his face was level with hers. Up close, he looked even more tired. There were shadows under his eyes like bruises.

“You did in one night what my people couldn’t do in two years,” he said. “I want you to read my routes.”

“No.”

“I’ll pay you more than your shop makes in a year. Every month.”

“No,” Elowen said again. “I sell flowers.”

He was quiet for a moment. Then he nodded, slowly, as if that was an answer he understood.

“Then listen to me,” he said. “Because nobody else will tell you this. Your father is safe from me. He isn’t safe from anyone else. The Qiu brothers know every route he has. And my men are going to remember that it was Lin Jian’s daughter who pointed at Kang. Kang had friends here. He bought them dinner for fifteen years.”

“Then protect him.”

“I don’t protect the people I pay.” He said it simply, without cruelty, like explaining that water was wet. “I pay them so they take the risk. That’s the deal. Your father knows the deal.”

“And who do you protect?”

Zhao didn’t answer straight away. The wind came off the water and moved his hair. Somewhere a crane groaned.

“What’s mine,” he said.

He stood up and closed the car door gently.

Through the glass, she watched him walk back across the yard, toward the door with the dusty pumps in the window. He didn’t look back.

Bao started the engine. “Home, Miss Lin?”

“Home,” she said.

All the way back through the city, she sat with her hands folded in her lap and listened to the words repeat in her head, quietly, over and over, like the forklift reversing in the warehouse.

I don’t protect the people I pay.

What’s mine.

By the time they reached the Walled City, she had stopped shaking, and she knew exactly what she was going to do.

chapters.title: A Proposal Made Like a Business Deal
chapters.desc: “Marry me. My father answers to you. In everything about my family, you answer to me.”
chapters.content:
Her father cried when she told him the debt was closed.

He didn’t cry the way he had cried at her mother’s funeral, with his whole body, folded over in the front row. He cried quietly, at the kitchen table, with his hands over his face, while Elowen stood at the stove with her back to him and pretended to be very busy with the kettle. She didn’t tell him about Kang. She didn’t tell him about the sound on the stairs. She told him that she had found a mistake in the papers, and Mr. Zhao had checked it, and it was not his fault.

“You went there,” Lin Jian said, when he could speak. “To the Docks. Alone.”

“Bao drove me home.”

“You know Bao’s name.” He lowered his hands. His eyes were red. “Elowen. What did you do?”

“I read your files.” She put a cup of tea in front of him. “You should change where you keep the key.”

He laughed, wetly, and then he stopped laughing, because he was a clever man under all the fear, and he had already thought of the thing she had been thinking about since the car.

“The Qiu brothers,” he said.

“Yes.”

“If Kang sold them my routes…”

“Yes.”

They sat in the kitchen and looked at each other, and neither of them said what they both knew. A fixer who loses his network has nothing left to sell. And a fixer whose daughter pointed at one of Zhao Zhendong’s oldest men has made enemies on both sides of the water.

✦ ✦ ✦

The warning came three days later.

Her father’s warehouse manager, a gentle, heavy man called Old Tan who had worked for them since before Elowen was born, didn’t come to work on Thursday. On Friday morning, a sanitation crew found him in an alley behind the fish market with both his legs broken and a piece of paper in his shirt pocket.

The paper said: LIN JIAN’S PEOPLE WALK SLOWLY NOW.

Elowen went to see him in hospital. He was asleep, grey under the lights, his legs in plaster to the hip. His wife sat beside the bed with a plastic bag of oranges in her lap that she had forgotten to put down. When she saw Elowen, she stood up and bowed, and kept saying thank you for coming, Miss Lin, thank you, as if Elowen had done something other than make this happen.

Elowen put a vase of chrysanthemums on the windowsill. Yellow, for recovery. Her hands were very steady.

That night her father didn’t come home until two. When he did, there was a new man in the car with him, someone she didn’t know, with a gun under his jacket.

“Protection,” Lin Jian said, not meeting her eyes. “I hired him.”

“With what money?”

He didn’t answer.

Upstairs, she could hear Eliana typing. Raiden’s light was still on. Evangeline’s door was open a crack, the way it always was when she couldn’t sleep, so she could hear the stairs.

Five children, Elowen thought. And one hired gun who would run the first time someone shot at him.

She went to her room and took out the delivery slip with the note she had written to herself a week ago. Iron Docks. 10 a.m. She turned it over and wrote on the back, carefully, in the neat handwriting she used for wedding cards:

Terms.

Then she sat at her desk until four in the morning, writing.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went back to the Docks at night, this time.

Bao was at the door again. He didn’t ask what she wanted. He looked at her face, opened the door, and said, “He’s upstairs. He hasn’t eaten.”

Zhao was alone. The long room was lit by one lamp on the desk. He was sitting with his feet on an open drawer, reading a binder, a cold box of rice beside him. The whiteboard had been wiped clean.

He looked up when she came in. He didn’t stand. He didn’t look surprised.

“Old Tan,” he said.

“You heard.”

“I hear everything that happens at the Docks.” He closed the binder. “I’m sorry about your man.”

She hadn’t expected that. It made the next part harder, so she said it quickly, before she lost her nerve.

“I want to make you an offer.”

He took his feet off the drawer.

Elowen didn’t sit down. She stood in front of the desk the way she stood in front of brides who wanted peonies in October, and she said the words she had practised all the way across the city.

“Marry me.”

The lamp buzzed faintly. Down in the warehouse, nothing moved.

Zhao Zhendong looked at her, and for the first time since she had known him, she saw him completely, honestly surprised. It lasted less than a second. Then his face went blank again, smooth as the wiped whiteboard behind him.

“Explain,” he said.

She took the folded paper from her bag and put it on the desk in front of him. He didn’t pick it up. He kept looking at her.

“You said you don’t protect the people you pay,” Elowen said. “You protect what’s yours. So I’ll be yours. On paper. If I’m your wife, my father isn’t just a man you pay. He’s your father-in-law. Your men won’t touch him. The Qiu brothers will have to think very hard before they touch anyone with my name.”

“And you think that’s worth something to me.”

“I think I’m worth something to you.” She made herself hold his eyes. “You offered me more than my shop makes in a year, every month, to read your routes. I’ll read them for nothing. I’ll find your leaks. I’ll tell you when your people lie on paper, because they do, and you’re too busy to check. And you’ll have a wife who runs a real business with real accounts and a real address in the Walled City. Not a woman you met at one of your clubs. A florist. Respectable. That’s useful to a man with your problems.”

“My problems.”

“Interpol,” Elowen said. “And whoever else. I read the newspapers.”

Something moved at the corner of his mouth again. That almost-smile.

“What else,” he said.

She pushed the paper toward him.

“Terms,” she said. “I keep my shop. My name stays on the sign. I work my own hours. I don’t come to your dinners unless I choose to. We have separate rooms. You don’t touch me unless I ask.” Her voice didn’t shake. She was proud of that. “And in everything that concerns my family—my father, my brothers and sisters—you answer to me. My father works for you. You will answer to me.”

Zhao finally picked up the paper. He unfolded it. It was three pages long, in her wedding-card handwriting, numbered.

He read every line. She watched him do it. He didn’t skim. When he reached the end, he went back to the beginning and read the first page again.

“Why not run?” he asked, without looking up.

“Where?”

“Anywhere. You have money. You could take the four of them and go.”

“And my father?”

He was quiet.

“You’d find us,” Elowen said. “If you wanted to. So would the Qiu brothers. And my father would stay, because he’s too proud and too frightened to leave, and the first time something went wrong at the Docks, someone would go to the house in the Walled City and find only him.” She swallowed. “I don’t run, Mr. Zhao. I cut things cleanly.”

He set the paper down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao Zhendong had been offered many things in his life.

Money, mostly. Guns, which he already had. Women, which he had never wanted when they were offered like a bottle of wine with the bill. Once, in the north, a general had offered him a racehorse. Once, a man about to die had offered him his own daughter, and Zhao had walked out of the room and never done business with him again.

Nobody had ever offered him themselves, with terms.

He looked at the woman standing in front of his desk. Her coat was buttoned wrong, one button off, all the way down. She hadn’t noticed. Her hands were folded tight in front of her. She was afraid of him, and she had come anyway, at night, alone, with three pages of rules in her neat handwriting, and she had looked him in the eye while she said you don’t touch me unless I ask.

He knew exactly what this was. It was a power play. It was a daughter putting herself between her father and a gun. It had nothing to do with him.

He found, to his surprise, that he didn’t care.

She’ll never love you, said a voice in the back of his head. It sounded like the guards at the detention centre, years ago. She’s buying you like you bought her flowers. You’ll spend the rest of your life wondering.

Yes, he thought. Probably.

He picked up a pen from the desk.

“One more term,” he said.

Elowen’s chin came up a little. “What?”

“You don’t lie to me.” He wrote it at the bottom of the third page, in his own blunt, square handwriting. “Lie to everyone else. Lie to your father, my men, the police, the newspapers. I don’t care. But not to me. Ever.”

She read the words twice.

“And you?” she said. “Will you lie to me?”

He thought about it honestly, which nobody had asked him to do in a long time.

“I’ll tell you when I can’t tell you something,” he said. “I won’t make something up.”

She nodded slowly.

“Then yes,” she said.

He signed the bottom of the page. Zhao Zhendong. Then he turned the paper around and held out the pen.

She took it. Her fingers touched his, briefly, and they were ice cold. She signed under his name. Lin Elowen. Her signature was small and very straight.

They looked at each other across the desk, over three pages that weren’t worth anything in any court, and both of them knew it was the most binding thing either of them had ever signed.

“Tuesday,” Zhao said. “The registry office opens at nine.”

“This Tuesday?”

“Old Tan is in hospital. Do you want to wait?”

She didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao drove her home again.

At the gate of the house in the Walled City, she looked down and finally noticed her coat was buttoned wrong, all the way down, and sat in the back of the car laughing silently into her hands until Bao asked, carefully, if she needed a doctor.

Upstairs, Zhao stayed at the desk long after she left.

He read the three pages again. Then he folded them along the creases she had made, put them in the inside pocket of his jacket, over his heart, and went back to his binder.

He didn’t eat the rice. He didn’t sleep.

At five in the morning, he called Chen Si.

“I’m getting married on Tuesday,” he said. “I need you to be a witness.”

On the other end of the line, for the first time in fifteen years, the most careful man Zhao knew was completely silent.

Then Chen Si said, “Is she pointing a gun at you?”

“No,” Zhao said. He looked at the folded paper, at the corner of it showing above his pocket. “Worse. She wrote a contract.”

chapters.title: Married at the Registry on a Tuesday
chapters.desc: A red-background photograph, soil under her nails, and a ring that is too heavy.
chapters.content:
To get married in the city, you needed four things: your identity card, three small photographs with a red background, a signed form saying you were not already married and not related to the person beside you, and your family’s household register.

The household register was a little red booklet that listed every person who lived in the Lin house. It belonged to the head of the household. It lived in the locked drawer in her father’s study, under the deeds to the house and her mother’s death certificate.

At three in the morning on Tuesday, Elowen took the key from behind the loose skirting board and opened the drawer.

Her hands were steady until she saw her mother’s certificate. The paper had gone soft at the folds. She sat on the floor with it for a minute, not reading it, just holding it, the way you hold someone’s hand in a hospital.

Then she put it back, took the household register, locked the drawer, and went to the flower market, because it was Tuesday, and on Tuesdays she bought ranunculus.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wholesale market opened at four. By five it was a roar of trolleys and plastic buckets and men shouting prices across the aisles. Elowen bought ranunculus and white roses and two boxes of eucalyptus from the old woman at the end stall, who had sold to her mother before her and who always slipped an extra bunch of something into her order without saying so.

“You look different,” the old woman said, counting change.

“I didn’t sleep.”

“That’s not it.” The old woman looked at her with sharp black eyes. “You look like a girl going to an exam.”

Elowen took the extra bunch. Today it was lily of the valley, out of season, very expensive. She didn’t know how the old woman had got it.

“In a way,” she said.

She drove the van back to the shop, unloaded, and processed everything: stripped the leaves, re-cut the stems, dropped them into buckets of cold water, put them in the cooler. She did it the way she always did, quickly and carefully, because flowers didn’t care what day it was. By eight her hands were green to the wrist and there was dirt under her nails that wouldn’t come out with a brush.

She changed into a cream blouse she kept at the shop for weddings. She looked at herself in the small mirror by the cooler. Then she took the lily of the valley out of its bucket, cut five stems short, and tied them with a piece of white ribbon.

She told herself it was so the old woman’s gift wouldn’t go to waste.

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry office was a grey government building near the river with a red banner over the door wishing everyone a harmonious family. There was a queue of couples on the steps: young ones holding hands, older ones who looked like they’d been arguing in the taxi, one boy in a suit so big it reached his knuckles.

Zhao Zhendong was standing at the bottom of the steps, a little apart from everyone else. Couples walked around him in a wide curve without knowing why.

He was wearing a dark blue suit that actually fitted, and a white shirt with no tie. He had shaved. He had also, she noticed, done something to his hair, and it had not gone well; one piece at the back was sticking up.

Beside him stood a man she had never met but recognised at once from the way Zhao’s body had turned slightly toward him, like a compass needle finding north.

Chen Si was a little older, a little shorter, and dressed in a grey suit that had obviously cost more than her van. He had a calm, handsome face and very watchful eyes, and he was holding a coffee cup that he had not drunk from.

“Miss Lin,” Chen Si said, with a small bow. “I am the witness.”

“Nobody needs a witness to register a marriage,” Elowen said. “It’s not in the regulations.”

“I know.” His mouth curved slightly. “I came anyway. I wanted to see this with my own eyes.”

Zhao looked at the lily of the valley in her hands. He looked at the dirt under her nails. Something in his face changed, and for a second he looked away.

“You went to the market,” he said.

“It’s Tuesday.”

“You went to the market,” he repeated, “before your wedding.”

“The ranunculus doesn’t know it’s my wedding.”

Chen Si made a small sound and turned it into a cough.

✦ ✦ ✦

The photographs came first.

There was a little booth inside, with a red curtain behind a bench and a bored young photographer with a big camera on a tripod. He sat them side by side and looked through the lens and sighed.

“Closer,” he said.

They moved two centimetres closer.

“Closer. You’re getting married, not filing taxes.”

Elowen moved until her shoulder touched Zhao’s arm. He went completely rigid, the way a dog goes rigid when a stranger puts a hand out, as though he was waiting to find out whether it would hurt.

“Lean your heads together,” said the photographer. “Groom, relax your face. You look like you’re about to rob me.”

Zhao didn’t relax his face. Elowen could feel how hard he was trying not to move. She thought about the contract. You don’t touch me unless I ask. He was holding himself so carefully that the arm against her shoulder felt like a piece of wood.

So she tilted her head and rested it, lightly, against his shoulder.

She felt him stop breathing.

“Good,” said the photographer. “Now smile. Both of you. One, two—”

The flash went off.

When the photographs came out of the machine, still warm, Chen Si leaned over and studied them.

In the picture, Elowen was smiling politely at the camera, her head on her husband’s shoulder, a little bunch of white flowers in her lap.

Zhao was not looking at the camera at all. He was looking down at her.

Chen Si took one of the spare prints, folded it neatly, and put it in his wallet without asking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The clerk was a middle-aged woman with reading glasses on a chain who had clearly married thousands of couples and expected nothing from any of them. She checked their identity cards, their forms, and the household register, stamping as she went. When she opened Elowen’s register and saw the long list of names, she glanced up.

“Five children,” she said. “Your father must be busy.”

“He is,” Elowen said.

The clerk turned to the last form, put her pen down, and looked at them over her glasses. It was the only part of the process that wasn’t paperwork, and she said it in a flat, practised voice, the way she must have said it ten thousand times.

“Are you both entering into this marriage of your own free will?”

“Yes,” said Elowen.

Zhao didn’t answer immediately.

The clerk waited. Chen Si, standing by the door with his untouched coffee, stopped pretending not to listen.

Zhao was looking at Elowen. Not at the clerk. At her. It was a question, she understood. The only one he would ask. Are you sure?

She met his eyes and nodded once.

“Yes,” Zhao said.

The clerk stamped two small red booklets with a sound like a door closing, pasted a photograph inside each one, and slid them across the desk.

“Congratulations,” she said, already reaching for the next folder. “Next.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside on the steps, in the thin spring sunlight, Zhao took a box out of his jacket pocket.

He didn’t kneel. He didn’t make a speech. He opened the box and held it out to her, and inside was a ring: a thick band of yellow gold with a square green stone set deep in it. It was old-fashioned and heavy and nothing like anything she would have chosen.

“I don’t know about rings,” he said. “I went to a jeweller yesterday. I told him I wanted something that wouldn’t break.”

She almost laughed. She didn’t, because his face was very serious, and because the ring was so plainly the ring of a man who had never been given anything that lasted.

She held out her left hand.

He took the ring out of the box. He looked at her hand, at the dirt under her nails, at the green stain on her fingers from the eucalyptus. Then he slid the ring on, and for one second his thumb stayed on her knuckle, rough and warm, as if he were checking that her hand was real.

It went over her knuckle and kept going. It was at least two sizes too big.

They both looked at it.

“I’ll get it fixed,” Zhao said.

“No.” She moved it to her middle finger. It fitted there, just. It was very heavy. “Leave it.”

Chen Si was smiling into his coffee cup.

“Aurelia is going to kill me,” he said, to nobody in particular, “for not letting her choose it.”

Elowen looked up sharply. “Aurelia?”

“My wife.” Chen Si’s smile widened, very slightly. “I believe you were at school together.”

Elowen stared at him. Then at Zhao, who had the expression of a man who had just remembered something he should have mentioned earlier.

Somewhere far away, in a different part of her mind, the seventeen-year-old who had once been called the Ice Queen in a school corridor heard the name Aurelia Song and put down everything she was holding.

“We’ll talk about that,” she said to her husband, “later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told her family that night.

She did it at dinner, because it was the only time they were all in one room, and because she had decided that if she was going to do something unforgivable, she would at least do it to their faces.

She put the little red booklet on the table, next to the fish.

Her father looked at it. He didn’t touch it. He looked at it the way he would look at a gun someone had placed on his dinner table.

“What is that,” he said.

“I got married today,” Elowen said. “To Zhao Zhendong.”

Nobody moved.

Then Lin Jian picked up the booklet, opened it, and saw the photograph, and his face went from white to grey to a deep dull red, and he slammed his hand down on the table so hard the dishes jumped.

“You sold yourself,” he said.

“No, Baba.” She didn’t raise her voice. “I bought you.”

“To that—that animal—”

“He’s your boss,” Elowen said. “You’ve worked for him for six years. You took his money and you put us through school with it. You don’t get to call him an animal at this table.”

Her father stood up so fast his chair fell over.

“I’ll have it annulled. I know people at the registry—”

“You’ll have to find the household register first,” said Elowen. “And then you’ll have to explain to Zhao Zhendong why you’re trying to take his wife away.”

Lin Jian stood there with his hand on the table, breathing hard, and for a moment she thought he might hit her. He never had. Not once in her life. But she had never seen his face like this.

Then he picked up his chair, set it back on its legs, sat down, and put his face in his hands.

Nobody spoke.

It was Raiden who finally moved. He reached across the table, picked up the booklet, and looked at the photograph. Then he looked at his sister.

“Does he know,” he said quietly, “that you’re the smartest person in this house?”

“He’s starting to.”

Raiden nodded slowly and put the booklet down.

From the stairs, a small voice said, “The registry office uploaded it at 11:42.”

They all turned. Eliana was sitting on the bottom step in her pyjamas with a laptop on her knees. She was seventeen and pale and her hair was a mess, and she looked at Elowen with enormous, frightened eyes.

“I saw it this morning,” she said. “I didn’t tell anyone. I thought it might be a mistake in the system.”

Evangeline got up from the table without a word. She walked around it, put her arms around Elowen from behind, and held on, her cheek pressed against her sister’s hair. She didn’t say anything. Evangeline almost never said anything. She just held on, very tightly, until Elowen felt something in her chest give way and had to close her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten o’clock, a car stopped outside the gate.

Her father went out before anyone could stop him.

Elowen watched from the window. She saw Zhao get out of the back seat. He was carrying a box, the kind flowers came in from the wholesaler. She saw her father walk right up to him, much closer than she had ever seen anyone stand to Zhao Zhendong, and say something, fast and furious, his finger jabbing at Zhao’s chest.

Zhao didn’t move. He didn’t step back. He let her father finish.

Then he said something, short. She couldn’t hear it.

Her father’s hand dropped. He stood in the light from the gate without moving. After a moment, he took the box from Zhao’s hands, turned around, and walked back into the house without looking at anyone.

He put the box on the kitchen table in front of Elowen.

Inside, packed carefully in wet paper, was a single bucket’s worth of tulips. Twenty stems. Red.

There was no note.

“What did he say to you?” Elowen asked her father.

Lin Jian looked at the tulips.

“I told him if he ever hurt you, I would kill him,” he said. “And he said you had already told him the same thing. In the shop. The night it rained.” Her father’s mouth twisted. “He said, ‘She told me she would find out where I sleep. I believe her.’”

Elowen looked down at the heavy ring on her middle finger.

“And then?”

“And then he said the tulips were to replace the ones he gave away.” Her father stood up slowly. He looked very old. “Go to bed, Elowen. You have to move house on Saturday.”

He went upstairs.

She sat at the kitchen table for a long time after everyone else had gone, with twenty red tulips and a red booklet and a ring that was two sizes too big.

She did not cry.

She put the tulips in water. She cut every stem at an angle with a knife, one inch from the bottom, the way you cut something so it will heal.

chapters.title: The House on the Hill Has Too Many Locks
chapters.desc: Separate rooms, two nameless dogs, her plants, and the one door she was not given a key to.
chapters.content:
Zhao Zhendong’s house stood on a hill above the Iron Docks, where the wind came straight off the water and smelled of salt and engines.

It was a big concrete box with long windows and a flat roof, the kind of house architects put in magazines. There was a gate with a camera on it, and a wall with another camera on it, and a gravel drive that announced every car long before it arrived. Two dogs came running down the drive when the van pulled in, lean and brown with black faces, and stopped exactly three metres from Elowen’s feet and stood there, quivering, staring at her.

“They won’t bite,” said Bao, getting out of the driver’s seat. “Unless he tells them.”

“What are their names?”

Bao looked at the dogs. He looked at her. He seemed genuinely surprised by the question.

“They don’t have names,” he said. “He calls them left and right.”

Elowen looked at the dogs. The dogs looked at her. One of them had a torn ear.

“That’s terrible,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had brought very little. Two suitcases of clothes. A box of books. Her mother’s jewellery box, which didn’t have much jewellery in it. And plants.

She had not meant to bring so many plants. She had started with the pothos from her bedroom windowsill, because it would die without her. Then the two orchids, because Evangeline had given them to her. Then the small lemon tree in its clay pot, because it had been her mother’s, and it had lived on the balcony of the house in the Walled City for twenty years, and she couldn’t imagine it there without her. Then a box of herbs. Then, at the last minute, a fern from the shop that was looking sorry for itself.

Zhao came out of the front door as Bao was lifting the lemon tree out of the van.

He was wearing an old grey sweatshirt and jeans, and he looked like a different person: younger, less sharp. He stopped on the top step and looked at the van. At the plants. At the lemon tree in Bao’s arms, with three small green lemons on it.

“That’s a tree,” he said.

“It’s my mother’s.”

He came down the steps and took the pot from Bao without a word. He carried it up into the house the way you would carry a sleeping child, both arms underneath it, looking down at it the whole time as if he was afraid it might fall out of the pot.

Inside, he stood in the middle of the hall, holding the tree, and turned in a slow circle.

“Where does it go?” he asked.

Elowen looked around the house.

It was enormous and almost empty. A long hall with a polished concrete floor. A living room with one black leather sofa, one television, and nothing else. No pictures on the walls. No rugs. No books. In the kitchen she could see a gleaming steel fridge and a counter with a single coffee cup on it.

It looked like a hotel that had closed.

“There,” she said, pointing at the end of the hall, where a long window looked out over the docks and the sea. “It needs light.”

He carried it there and set it down, and then stood back and looked at it, a lemon tree in a clay pot in his concrete hall, with a frown on his face like a man trying to solve a problem.

“Does it need anything?” he said.

“Water once a week. Don’t let it get cold.”

He nodded slowly, as if memorising it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He showed her the house the way an estate agent might have, if the estate agent had been trained by the army.

“This door locks from inside. This one too. That window doesn’t open; it’s bulletproof. These ones open but there’s a sensor. If they open between midnight and six, Bao knows. This panel turns on the lights in the garden. This one is a phone that only rings in the guardhouse.”

There were fourteen locks on the ground floor. She counted.

Upstairs, there were four bedrooms. He opened the door to the biggest one, at the end of the corridor, with its own bathroom and a wide window over the sea, and stood back to let her go in first.

The bed was made with new white sheets. The tags were still on the pillows. On the bedside table there was a glass vase with nothing in it, as if someone had known a vase was supposed to be there but hadn’t known what to put in it.

“This is yours,” he said.

She looked around. There was a dent in the carpet where a different bed had stood until very recently.

“This was your room.”

He didn’t answer.

“Where are you sleeping?”

He walked back down the corridor and opened the smallest door, the one right at the top of the stairs. Inside there was a narrow bed, a chair, and a window that looked down on the front gate.

“Here,” he said.

“That’s the worst room in the house.”

“It’s the first room anyone reaches,” said Zhao, “if they come up the stairs.”

She looked at him, standing in the doorway of the little room with his hands in the pocket of his sweatshirt, and understood what he meant. He had given her the room at the end, and put himself between her and the stairs.

She didn’t thank him. It didn’t seem like the kind of thing you thanked someone for. She said, “The dogs need names,” and went back down to get the orchids.

✦ ✦ ✦

The keys were on a ring on the kitchen counter when she came back from unloading. Thirteen of them, each with a little coloured tag.

“Thirteen,” she said. “You have fourteen locks.”

Zhao was standing at the kitchen window, drinking coffee. He didn’t turn around.

“The basement,” he said. “You don’t need that one.”

“What’s in the basement?”

He was quiet for a moment. “I’ll tell you when I can tell you something,” he said, “and I won’t make anything up. That was the deal.”

“So this is one of the things you can’t tell me.”

“Not today.”

She looked at the thirteen keys. Then at his back. Then she picked up the ring and put it in her pocket, and didn’t ask again.

Dinner was takeaway from a place near the Docks: rice, braised pork, a soup with too much salt. Bao brought it in plastic boxes. They ate at the kitchen counter, standing up, because there were no chairs at the counter and the dining table in the next room had nothing on it but dust.

Zhao ate very fast, without looking at the food, like someone who had learned to eat before anyone could take it away.

“There’s a dining table,” Elowen said.

“I know.”

“Have you ever used it?”

He thought about it. “Once. Chen Si came for New Year.”

“And you sat at it?”

“He sat at it.”

She put her chopsticks down. “Tomorrow,” she said, “I’m cooking. And we’re sitting down.”

He looked at her as if she had said something in a foreign language. Then he nodded, once, the way he had nodded at the lemon tree. Water once a week. Don’t let it get cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

She couldn’t sleep.

The house made the wrong noises. In the Walled City there had always been sound: neighbours, scooters, the old man next door who sang opera to his birds. Here there was only wind, and the far-off groan of the cranes, and every so often the crunch of gravel as a guard walked the wall.

At two in the morning she heard a door open.

She lay still and listened. Footsteps on the stairs, going down. Not sneaking. Just quiet, the way a man walks in his own house when he doesn’t want to wake anyone. Then another door, further away, deeper. A heavy sound, metal on metal. A lock.

She got up.

She didn’t decide to. Her feet decided. She went down the stairs in her socks, past the lemon tree glowing faintly in the light from the docks, through the kitchen to a door she had noticed earlier and assumed was a pantry.

It was open. Behind it, concrete stairs went down. At the bottom, there was light.

She went halfway down and stopped.

The basement ran the whole length of the house. It was very clean and very bright, and along both walls, in steel racks, there were guns. Not a few. Dozens. Long rifles in neat rows, pistols in foam-lined drawers, boxes stacked to the ceiling with stencilled numbers on their sides. It smelled of oil and metal and something sharp, like a hardware shop.

In the middle of the room there was a long workbench under a hanging lamp, and Zhao was sitting at it with his back to her.

He was cleaning a pistol.

He had taken it apart and laid the pieces out on a cloth in a straight line, and he was working on them one at a time with a small brush and a rag. Slowly, piece by piece. His shoulders were loose in a way she hadn’t seen before, as if this was the only place in the house where he could put something down.

She must have made a sound.

He didn’t jump. He didn’t turn around fast. He put down the brush, and the piece of metal in his other hand, and then he turned on his stool and looked at her standing halfway down his stairs in her pyjamas.

Neither of them spoke.

“I couldn’t sleep,” Elowen said.

“Neither could I.”

She looked at the racks. At the boxes. She thought about the long crates in her father’s garage when she was a child, and the men with accents from countries she couldn’t find on the map.

“Are these what you sell?”

“No.” He looked at the racks too. “What I sell never comes to this house. These are mine. For if someone comes here.” He paused. “For if someone comes here for you.”

She came down the rest of the stairs.

Up close, the pieces on the cloth were small and black and oiled, and they didn’t look like anything. They looked like parts of a sewing machine.

“Why at two in the morning?” she asked.

Zhao picked up the rag again and turned it over in his hands.

“When I was sixteen,” he said, “the only thing in my life that did what it was supposed to do was a gun. You clean it, you put it back together, it works. Every time.” He shrugged, one shoulder. “People don’t.”

It was the most he had ever said to her about himself.

She stood beside the workbench and watched him put the pistol back together, piece by piece, without looking at his hands. It took him less than a minute. When he was finished, he put it in a drawer and closed it, and then he got up, went to the wall by the door, and wrote something on the back of a business card with a pen from his pocket.

He held the card out to her.

It was six numbers.

“This door,” he said. “It’s steel. The walls are concrete. There’s water down here, and a phone line that doesn’t go through the house, and air that comes from outside.” He kept holding out the card. “If anyone ever comes into this house who isn’t me or Bao, you come here. You close the door. You put in that code from the inside. And you wait.”

“For how long?”

“For me.”

She took the card.

Their fingers touched on it. His were warm from the lamp and smelled of gun oil, and he didn’t let go straight away. For a second they stood holding the same small card between them under the hanging light, close enough that she could see a nick on his lower lip she had never noticed, and the pulse moving in his throat.

Then he let go.

“You said I didn’t need the basement key.”

“You don’t need a key,” said Zhao. “You need the code. I just didn’t want you to have a reason to use it.”

He turned off the lamp over the workbench, and they went back up the stairs together, him behind her, the way he had put himself at the top of the stairs.

At the door of the little room by the stairs, he stopped.

“Goodnight, Elowen,” he said.

It was the first time he had said her name without Miss Lin in front of it. It sounded strange in his voice, careful, as if he were holding something that might break.

“Goodnight,” she said.

She went down the corridor to the big room at the end, and closed the door, and sat on the bed with the card in her hand.

In the morning, before he was awake, she went out to the garden with a bowl of leftover pork. The dogs came running and stopped exactly three metres away, the way they had been trained.

“You,” she said to the one with the torn ear, “are Dumpling. And you are Noodle.”

The dogs stared at her.

From the window of the little room at the top of the stairs, a man who had been awake since five watched his wife feed his guard dogs breakfast, and did not go back to bed.

chapters.title: Breakfast With a Man Who Eats Standing Up
chapters.desc: She makes him sit down. He starts driving her to the market at four.
chapters.content:
On Sunday she cleaned the dining table.

It took most of the morning. The dust had settled into the grain of the wood, and there were rings on it from a glass someone had put down years ago and nobody had wiped up. She found a cloth and a bucket under the sink, still in their plastic wrapping, and scrubbed until the table shone. Then she found six chairs in a cupboard, still wrapped in plastic too, and took four of them out.

Zhao came downstairs at noon and stopped in the doorway of the dining room as if he had walked into the wrong house.

“You cleaned it,” he said.

“I said we’d sit down.”

“I thought you meant it as a—” He searched for the word. “A figure of speech.”

“I don’t use figures of speech about dinner.”

She cooked in the afternoon. The kitchen was beautiful and completely unused: an enormous gas stove, a steel fridge with nothing in it but beer and eggs and a bottle of chilli sauce, cupboards full of white plates that had never been out of their boxes. She sent Bao to the market with a list. He came back with everything on it and a bag of mandarins she hadn’t asked for.

“For the house,” he said, very seriously, putting them in a bowl on the counter. “A house should have fruit.”

She made her mother’s dishes. Tomato and egg, because everyone could eat it. Steamed fish with ginger and spring onion. Green beans fried with garlic. Rice. A soup of pork bones and lotus root that needed three hours, and filled the house with a smell that made both the dogs sit outside the kitchen door with their noses pressed to the glass.

At seven, she put it all on the table, and called him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in and stood beside his chair.

He looked at the food. He looked at the chair. He looked at her, already sitting, with her napkin in her lap.

For a moment she thought he wasn’t going to do it. He stood there like a man who had been asked to sit in an electric chair.

Then he pulled the chair out, slowly, and sat down.

He sat very straight. He put his hands on the table on either side of his bowl and didn’t pick up his chopsticks. He looked, she thought, exactly like a boy in a school canteen who had been told off for eating too fast and was now afraid to eat at all.

She served him fish, the best piece from the belly, and put it in his bowl.

He looked at it.

“My mother always gave my father the belly,” she said. “He gave it back to her. Every night, for twenty years. They never ate it.”

Zhao picked up his chopsticks. He ate the fish. Slowly, for once.

They didn’t talk much. She asked how long he had lived in the house. Three years. She asked who had designed it. A man from the south who owed him money. She asked if he had any family.

He put down his chopsticks.

“No,” he said.

She waited.

“I was adopted,” he said. “From an orphanage in the north. By a man who wanted someone to carry steel at his yard. He died when I was fourteen. Then I was on my own. Then I was somewhere I wasn’t supposed to be, and I met Chen Si.” He picked up the chopsticks again. “That’s my family.”

It was said so flatly that she didn’t know what to say back. So she said the only thing she could think of, which was true.

“The soup is better on the second day.”

He looked up.

“Then we’ll eat it tomorrow,” he said. “Sitting down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her alarm went off at three-thirty on Monday morning.

She dressed in the dark, in jeans and an old jumper and her market boots. She tied her hair up. She picked up the van keys from the bowl by the front door, next to the mandarins.

The van keys weren’t there.

She stood in the hall, looking at the bowl, trying to remember if she had left them in the van. Then she heard a small noise from the kitchen and went to look.

Zhao was standing at the counter, fully dressed, drinking coffee. He had a second cup beside him, already poured. The van keys were in his other hand.

“No,” said Elowen.

“It’s four in the morning,” said Zhao. “The road down to the market goes past the Qiu brothers’ warehouse. You’re not driving it alone.”

“I’ve driven to the market alone every day for five years.”

“You weren’t my wife for five years.” He held out the coffee. “Bao’s asleep. I’ll drive.”

She looked at him. He looked back, patient and immovable, like a wall.

“The contract says I work my own hours.”

“It does.” He didn’t lower the coffee. “It doesn’t say anything about who drives.”

She thought about arguing. Then she thought about the Qiu brothers’ warehouse, and Old Tan in the hospital bed with his legs in plaster to the hip.

She took the coffee.

“You carry the buckets,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wholesale flower market was in a long, low building by the river, with metal shutters that rolled up at four and the smell of wet greenery and diesel pouring out into the dark. The car park was full of vans. Inside, under bare fluorescent lights, a hundred stalls stood shoulder to shoulder, piled with boxes and buckets: roses from the south, lilies from the hothouses outside the city, chrysanthemums by the thousand, carnations in every colour that existed and several that didn’t.

Elowen loved it. She had loved it since she was eight and her mother had brought her here half-asleep, wrapped in a coat, and bought her a hot soy milk from the man at the door.

She walked in like she always did, quickly, with her list in her head.

The market went quiet behind her.

Not completely. The trolleys kept rattling and somewhere a radio kept playing. But the shouting stopped. Prices stopped being called across the aisles. Men who had been arguing over boxes of gypsophila went silent and turned their faces away.

She looked back.

Zhao was walking two steps behind her with his hands in his pockets, looking at the flowers with polite interest. He was not doing anything. He did not need to do anything.

“You’re frightening everybody,” she said.

“I’m walking.”

“Walk less frighteningly.”

He considered this. Then he took his hands out of his pockets, which somehow made it worse.

At the old woman’s stall at the end of the aisle, the old woman looked up from her stool, saw who was standing behind Elowen, and very slowly put down her cigarette.

“Granny Su,” said Elowen. “This is my husband.”

Granny Su looked Zhao up and down. He stood there and let her. Then she looked at the ring on Elowen’s middle finger.

“Too big,” Granny Su said.

“I know,” said Zhao.

“Get it fixed.”

“She won’t let me.”

Granny Su picked her cigarette back up and pointed it at him. “Then you carry. Twenty boxes. The eucalyptus is heavy. Don’t crush the stems.”

Elowen had never in her life seen anyone give Zhao Zhendong an order. She watched him pick up the first box of eucalyptus, with both arms underneath, as if it might break.

“Not like that,” said Granny Su. “Like you’re carrying it, not like it’s a baby.”

He adjusted his grip.

✦ ✦ ✦

She learned something about him that morning, which was that he noticed everything.

At the third stall, a man she had bought roses from for two years counted out ten bunches, wrapped, and named a price. Elowen reached for her purse.

“That bunch,” said Zhao.

The man looked up. Then he looked at who was speaking, and his face went white.

Zhao reached past Elowen, picked up the fourth bunch from the stack, and held it up. “Count it.”

“Sir, I—”

“Count it.”

The man counted, his hands shaking. There were eighteen stems. A standard bunch of roses was twenty.

Zhao put it down and picked up the next one. Eighteen again. And the next.

By the end there were nineteen missing roses across ten bunches. Elowen stood with her purse half open and did the sum: nineteen roses a day, six days a week, for two years.

“I’m sorry, I’m so sorry, Miss Lin, it was a mistake, the packer—” The man was babbling. He was looking at Zhao, not at her. “I’ll make it right, I’ll give you—”

“Don’t talk to me,” said Zhao quietly. “Talk to her. She’s the one you were stealing from.”

The man turned to Elowen. Up close, she could see sweat on his upper lip. He was terrified, completely and physically terrified, of a man who had done nothing but count roses.

She thought about the stairs at the Docks. The sound.

“Give me the missing stems,” she said. “From now on, I count every bunch. If it happens again, I buy somewhere else.” She paused. “That’s all.”

The man nodded so hard she thought his neck might hurt.

When they had walked away, out of earshot, she said, “You didn’t need to do that.”

“He was stealing from you.”

“I would have found out.”

“When?” Zhao asked, and when she didn’t answer, he said, “That’s why I did it.”

She stopped in the aisle and looked at him. A woman pushing a trolley of lilies went round them in a wide curve.

“If you scare every person who cheats me,” Elowen said, “nobody in this market will ever talk to me normally again.”

He thought about that. She could see him thinking about it, actually thinking, turning it over like the pieces of the pistol on the cloth.

“Then tell me,” he said finally, “when you want me to stand somewhere else.”

“Now,” said Elowen. “By the door. With the soy milk man.”

He went and stood by the door with the soy milk man.

When she came out twenty minutes later with the rest of her order, he was holding two cups of hot soy milk and the soy milk man was telling him, at great length, about his son’s university entrance exam.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the drive back, the sky over the river began to go grey.

She meant to stay awake. She always stayed awake. But the car was warm and quiet, and he drove differently from Bao, smoothly, without any sudden braking, and somewhere on the long road past the Qiu brothers’ dark warehouse her head tipped against the window and she slept.

When she woke, they were parked outside the shop, and his jacket was over her, tucked in around her shoulders. It smelled of coffee and cold air and something that was only him. She didn’t remember him putting it there. She lay against the window for a moment longer than she needed to, pretending she was still asleep. The engine was off. The street was still empty. The clock on the dashboard said 6:14.

He was sitting with his hands on the wheel, looking straight ahead.

“How long have we been here?” she asked.

“Twenty minutes.”

“You should have woken me.”

“You were asleep,” said Zhao, as if that were the end of the argument.

He carried the buckets in. He didn’t know where anything went, so he stood in the middle of the shop holding twenty boxes of eucalyptus until she told him, and then he put them exactly where she said, lined up straight.

She made breakfast on the hot plate in the back: two fried eggs on rice with soy sauce, the only thing she ever had time for on market days. She put one plate on the counter for him.

He picked it up and started to eat, standing, by the door.

“There’s a stool,” she said, pointing.

He looked at the stool behind the counter. Then at her. Then, without a word, he sat down on it, with the plate on his knees, and ate his fried eggs sitting down in a flower shop at half past six in the morning, his shoulders slowly coming down from around his ears.

When he finished, he washed the plate in the little sink at the back. He dried it. He put it away in the wrong place.

At the door, he stopped.

“Tomorrow,” he said. “Same time.”

It wasn’t a question.

“The contract—” Elowen started.

“Says you work your own hours,” said Zhao. “I know. I’m not working. I’m driving.”
